subject: history
topicDisplay: Ideas, political power, industry and empire: Britain, 1745-1901
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 history question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: The Enlightenment and new ideas about reason and rights
Britain as the first industrial nation and the Industrial Revolution
Urbanisation and working conditions in industrial towns
The transatlantic slave trade and the triangular trade
Abolition of the slave trade (1807) and slavery (1833) and its campaigners
Britain's empire and its growth in India and Africa
Political power, protest and the campaign for the vote (Great Reform Act 1832, Chartism)

questions.lo: The Enlightenment and new ideas about reason and rights
questions.q: What did Enlightenment thinkers argue should guide how we understand the world and run society?
questions.explain: The Enlightenment championed reason, science and evidence over blind tradition. This encouraged people to question authorities like the divine right of kings and to talk about rights and liberty.

questions.lo: The Enlightenment and new ideas about reason and rights
questions.q: How did Enlightenment ideas help later campaigners against slavery and for the vote?
options: They gave people the language of rights and equality to argue for reform
questions.explain: Enlightenment ideas about liberty, rights and equality gave reformers the arguments they used to challenge slavery and to demand a wider vote.

questions.lo: Britain as the first industrial nation and the Industrial Revolution
questions.q: Which of these best describes the Industrial Revolution in Britain?
options: A gradual change over many decades, with factories, steam and railways
A single event that happened in one year
A movement to return to farming
questions.explain: Britain was the first industrial nation. The change was gradual, spread over many decades, as work moved into factories powered by coal and steam, and railways connected the country. Thinking it happened overnight is a common mistake.

questions.lo: Britain as the first industrial nation and the Industrial Revolution
questions.q: Which power source drove many of the new factories of the Industrial Revolution?
questions.explain: Coal-fired steam engines powered the machines in the new factories, which is why coal and iron were so important to industrial Britain.

questions.lo: Urbanisation and working conditions in industrial towns
questions.q: Why did industrial towns such as Manchester grow so quickly?
options: People moved from the countryside for factory jobs (urbanisation)
The government forced everyone to move
questions.explain: Factories built in towns created jobs, so people moved in from the countryside to find work. This rush of people into towns is called urbanisation, and it led to overcrowding and poor living conditions.

questions.lo: Urbanisation and working conditions in industrial towns
questions.q: Which of these was a common problem for workers in early industrial cities?
options: Long hours, child labour and disease from overcrowding
questions.explain: Rapid growth meant overcrowding, poor sanitation and disease such as cholera, while workers often faced very long hours and child labour before later reforms improved conditions.

questions.lo: The transatlantic slave trade and the triangular trade
questions.q: In the triangular trade, what were enslaved African people forced to endure on the middle leg across the Atlantic?
options: The brutal 'Middle Passage' to the Americas
A journey back to Britain to be freed
questions.explain: In the triangular trade, ships carried goods to Africa, then enslaved people across the Atlantic in the brutal Middle Passage, and finally sugar, cotton and tobacco back to Britain for large profits.

questions.lo: The transatlantic slave trade and the triangular trade
questions.q: Where were most enslaved Africans forced to work after being transported across the Atlantic?
options: Plantations in the Caribbean and the Americas
questions.explain: Most enslaved people were forced to work on plantations growing crops such as sugar, cotton and tobacco in the Caribbean and the Americas.

questions.lo: Abolition of the slave trade (1807) and slavery (1833) and its campaigners
questions.q: What was abolished across the British Empire in 1807?
options: The slave trade (buying and shipping enslaved people)
questions.explain: In 1807 the slave TRADE was abolished. Slavery ITSELF was not abolished across the British Empire until 1833 - the two dates are easy to confuse.

questions.lo: Abolition of the slave trade (1807) and slavery (1833) and its campaigners
questions.q: Which statement about abolition is most accurate?
options: It took decades, with the trade ended in 1807 and slavery in 1833
It all happened in a single year
It was achieved with no campaigning
Slavery was ended before the slave trade
questions.explain: Abolition was a long campaign led by figures such as Olaudah Equiano, William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson. The trade ended in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833 - a gap of decades.

questions.lo: Abolition of the slave trade (1807) and slavery (1833) and its campaigners
questions.q: Who was Olaudah Equiano?
options: A formerly enslaved writer who campaigned against slavery
questions.explain: Olaudah Equiano was a formerly enslaved African whose writing and speaking helped the abolition campaign by showing the reality of slavery.

questions.lo: Britain's empire and its growth in India and Africa
questions.q: Which country, ruled directly by Britain from 1858, became central to the empire and was called the 'jewel in the crown'?
questions.explain: India was central to the British Empire. From 1858 it was ruled directly by the British government (the Raj), and Queen Victoria was later titled Empress of India.

questions.lo: Britain's empire and its growth in India and Africa
questions.q: Why was it said that 'the sun never set' on the British Empire by 1901?
options: It was so large it stretched right around the globe
It was made entirely of deserts
questions.explain: By 1901 the British Empire was the largest the world had seen, spread across so many parts of the globe that it was always daytime somewhere within it.

questions.lo: Political power, protest and the campaign for the vote (Great Reform Act 1832, Chartism)
questions.q: What did the Great Reform Act of 1832 do?
options: Removed some rotten boroughs and gave the vote to more middle-class men
Gave the vote to every adult in Britain
questions.explain: The 1832 Act removed some 'rotten boroughs', gave seats to growing industrial towns and extended the vote to more middle-class men. It did NOT give the vote to most working men or to any women.

questions.lo: Political power, protest and the campaign for the vote (Great Reform Act 1832, Chartism)
questions.q: What did the Chartists demand in the People's Charter from 1838?
options: Reforms such as the vote for all adult men and a secret ballot
A return to rule by the Church
questions.explain: Chartism was Britain's first mass political movement. Its People's Charter demanded reforms including votes for all adult men and a secret ballot; most of these demands were eventually met in later years.

questions.lo: Political power, protest and the campaign for the vote (Great Reform Act 1832, Chartism)
questions.q: Which statement about the right to vote in this period is correct?
options: The vote was widened in stages over many decades
The 1832 Act gave everyone the vote at once
questions.explain: The vote expanded like climbing a ladder, one rung at a time - the 1832, 1867 and 1884 reforms each widened it, but full democracy came only in the 20th century.

questions.lo: Ireland and the Union
questions.q: What did the Act of Union of 1801 create?
options: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
questions.explain: The 1801 Act of Union joined Ireland with Great Britain to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with Irish MPs sitting in the Parliament in London.

questions.lo: Ireland and the Union
questions.q: Which disaster in the 1840s caused mass death and emigration in Ireland?
questions.explain: The Great Famine of the 1840s caused enormous death and emigration in Ireland and deepened tensions with Britain.

questions.lo: Victorian society and reform
questions.q: What did the Victorian Factory Acts aim to do?
options: Limit working hours and restrict child labour
questions.explain: The Factory Acts were reforms that gradually limited working hours and child labour, part of a slow, hard-won improvement in industrial life alongside public health and education reforms.

questions.lo: Victorian society and reform
questions.q: What do the campaigns to abolish slavery and to widen the vote have in common?
options: Both were long reform campaigns that achieved change gradually, in stages
Both were completed in a single year
Both were led only by kings
questions.explain: Both drew on Enlightenment ideas of rights and equality and both achieved change slowly, step by step, over many years rather than all at once.
